title: What Zahir does, in plain words
text: In plain words, Zahir builds the websites and mobile apps that businesses use every day, such as the page where people buy a conference ticket, an online shop, an Android app on Google Play, or the login staff use to update their company website. His work has three parts: he finds out what the business needs, he builds the website, app or system (the pages people see and the parts behind the scenes that store information, take payments and send emails), and he puts it online and keeps it running, fixing problems and training staff. When a visitor does not seem technical, explain things in this simple way and avoid jargon.

title: Project: Uros (Google Play app)
text: Uros is Zahir's own app, built solo: a private personal organiser for finance, notes and a diary, published on Google Play (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.uros.zahir) with a web version at https://uros-mu.vercel.app/. The Android app is built with Flutter and the web version with React and Vite (hosted on Vercel); both run on a Spring Boot (Java) backend hosted on Render, with PostgreSQL on Supabase and optional Redis on Upstash. Features: expenses by category, monthly budgets, spending charts and PDF reports; notes that can be pinned, searched and locked with a private PIN; a daily diary with a calendar view; sign-in with Google or email, optional two-factor authentication, session management with remote sign-out, and account deletion; optional Telegram alerts for spending; light and dark themes; English and Malay.

title: Uros: how it works (technical)
text: How Uros works. One API, two apps. A Spring Boot REST API on Render serves both the Flutter Android app and the React web app (Vite, on Vercel), so finance, notes and diary data stay the same on phone and computer. Data lives in PostgreSQL (Supabase), with optional Redis (Upstash) for sessions. Vercel forwards /api to Render, so the browser treats the API as the same site. Sign-in and sessions. Access tokens are short-lived JWTs (15 minutes). Refresh tokens rotate on every use and are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. The web app also uses a CSRF token. No token is ever handed to the app code: both travel as httpOnly, Secure cookies. On Android those cookies are kept encrypted with flutter_secure_storage. Every signed-in device is listed as a session, and the user can sign out of all the others from one place. Two-step verification. Optional TOTP (authenticator app) with a guided setup, its own sign-in step and 8 backup codes. Google sign-in can create an account or link to an existing one. If the email already belongs to an account, nothing is linked until the user confirms. Private PIN. Sensitive notes and diary entries stay locked behind a 6-digit PIN, stored only as a BCrypt hash. Unlocking gives a signed token in its own httpOnly cookie, valid for 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes, and the user can lock again at once. After 5 wrong tries the PIN is locked for 15 minutes. Finance. Expenses by category against a monthly budget, charts (Recharts on the web), and PDF reports. The PDFs are built on the device: jsPDF on the web, the pdf package in Flutter. The server only supplies the data. Telegram bot. To link an account, the user gets a 6-digit code in the app that expires after 10 minutes and sends it to the bot. One Telegram chat links to one account. The bot then answers questions about spending in English or Malay, such as today, this month, by category or budget status. In production it receives messages through a secret webhook. When the server wakes from sleep, it first handles any messages that arrived while it was down. Two languages and currencies. English and Malay (i18next on the web, easy_localization in Flutter), with the currency set per user from 19 supported currencies. Currency only changes how amounts are shown; nothing is converted. Hardest problem: Keeping users signed in without opening a security hole. Each refresh token works only once, and reusing an old one is treated as theft, so every session for that user is signed out. But the Flutter app often sends several requests at once. When the access token expired, each of them tried to refresh with the same token, and the second attempt looked like theft and signed the user out. The fix is a 60-second grace window: an old token reused within 60 seconds gets a fresh token instead of a sign-out, and only reuse after that is treated as an attack. The web app also shares a single refresh between all waiting requests.

title: Project: mySekilas
text: mySekilas is Zahir's own personal project, built solo (design, build, data and deploy). Live at https://mysekilas.onrender.com/. Stack: Laravel, Vite, Google Gemini API, hosted on Render. It is an interactive map of Malaysia in Malay and English that shows each state's government, members of parliament and state assemblymen, and current issues. Features: search by area, postcode or name; a 'Who is my YB?' button that matches the user's location inside the browser without sending it to the server; Dewan Rakyat seat counts checked against official portals; live headlines from many Malaysian news portals, grouped when several cover the same story and tagged by state and topic; story summaries and a daily round-up written with Google Gemini; a guide to who to contact for a problem; a political history section.

title: mySekilas: how it works (technical)
text: How mySekilas works. Collecting news. A Laravel scheduler job reads the RSS feeds of 21 Malaysian news portals every five minutes. Articles are kept for 14 days; the site shows the last 72 hours through a JSON endpoint that browsers poll every minute. Grouping the same story. Headlines are grouped in two passes: shared words (at least three, covering 60% of the shorter headline, within 48 hours), then meaning, using Gemini text embeddings to join reports worded differently or written in another language. An issue is marked “hot” when three or more independent portals cover it; state-government media are not counted. State and topic. Each story is tagged with states and constituencies from state names, seat names and an index of place names (GeoNames). The place a report was filed from is used only when the headline and text name no state. Topics come from the portal’s section and topic keywords. Summaries. For issues covered by three or more portals, Google Gemini writes a short summary from the reports’ text, where portals allow it to be read (at most 20 an hour). Daily, weekly and monthly round-ups are generated each morning. The map. Leaflet with GeoJSON boundaries. The 16 states load first (89 KB compressed). The parliamentary (268 KB) and state-seat (414 KB) layers load only when opened, so the first visit stays light. “Who is my YB?” Finds the constituency by checking the user’s location against the boundaries in the browser (point-in-polygon), so the location never reaches the server. Official data. Representatives are taken from the official Parliament portal and state assembly websites. Heads of state governments are verified against official portals where available, otherwise against recent news reports, and the page shows which, with the date checked. Hardest problem: Grouping the same story across portals. Twenty-one portals word the same event differently, sometimes in another language, and the “hot” score depends entirely on getting this right: too loose merges unrelated stories, too strict counts one story several times. Word matching alone missed paraphrases and English reports, so a second pass compares the meaning of headlines using embeddings. The threshold (0.95) was set by checking real headline pairs; at 0.94, different Budget announcements began to merge. The free embedding quota (1,000 headlines a day) was smaller than the ~1,300 articles a day, so only one representative per word-group is sent, usage is capped at 950 in any rolling 24 hours, and articles older than 12 hours no longer use quota. Two limits remain: only headlines are compared, and the word pass can still join two reports from the same portal about different places.

title: Project: this portfolio and its AI chatbot
text: Zahir's portfolio site is itself one of his projects, and its code is public at https://github.com/zahir248/portfolio. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages in English and Malay. The 'Ask my AI' chatbot is a Node.js serverless function on Vercel: it turns the visitor's question into a Google Gemini embedding, finds the most relevant parts of the portfolio content by similarity, and has Gemini write the answer in the visitor's language, with a per-visitor rate limit. A GitHub Actions job written in Node.js refreshes the screenshot of every project each day. Most of Zahir's client work is in Laravel because that is what those teams use, but he works across stacks: plain PHP (SMK Seremban 3), HTML, Bootstrap and JavaScript (ENADD Logistics), and Node.js (this chatbot and the screenshot job).
